item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q021_nad_binding_convergent_evolution","answer":"NAD or NADP use is not a SCOPe homology statement by itself. In SCOPe, the canonical NAD(P)-binding Rossmann domain is the alpha/beta fold `c.2`, with many dehydrogenase families under the Rossmann-fold superfamily `c.2.1`; however, NAD(P)-dependent enzymes also occur in other SCOPe folds and superfamilies. That distribution means the ability to bind the nicotinamide dinucleotide has been acquired more than once: members inside a single SCOPe family are plausible close homologs, members grouped in one SCOPe superfamily such as `c.2.1` are inferred to be remotely homologous despite family-level divergence, but NAD(P)-binding proteins placed in different SCOPe folds or unrelated superfamilies should be treated as independent, convergent solutions unless there is stronger structural evidence for common ancestry. Cofactor binding alone is unsafe for transferring homology because NAD(P) is a common metabolite with a constrained ADP-ribose/nicotinamide geometry, so unrelated alpha/beta scaffolds can evolve phosphate-, ribose-, or nicotinamide-contacting loops in comparable positions. The same caveat applies to local active-site similarity: a short glycine-rich dinucleotide-binding motif, a catalytic acid/base, or a similar hydride-transfer arrangement may reflect chemistry and ligand geometry rather than shared ancestry. Thus an NAD(P)-bound template from another fold can suggest possible residues to inspect or a coarse docking pose, but it should not be used to assign family or superfamily membership, infer divergent evolution, or transfer detailed substrate specificity/catalytic mechanism without global fold agreement and SCOPe-level homology evidence.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]}]}
